### 1960s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1960s")]

Prominent conservative author and commentator [William F. Buckley Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_F._Buckley_Jr. "William F. Buckley Jr.") ran for [Mayor of New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayor_of_New_York_City "Mayor of New York City") on the Conservative Party line in [1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_New_York_City_mayoral_election "1965 New York City mayoral election"), winning 13.4% of the vote.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-3) An op-ed in _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ described the Buckley campaign as "a watershed campaign for the Conservatives, who gained heavy publicity and proved their strength in the overwhelmingly Democratic city."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto-2) In 1966, Conservative candidate Paul L. Adams obtained more than half a million votes in his race for Governor of New York,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto1-4) winning Row C for the Party.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto2-5)

### 1970s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1970s")]

In [1970](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_election_in_New_York,_1970 "United States Senate election in New York, 1970"), [James Buckley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_L._Buckley "James L. Buckley"), the brother of William F. Buckley Jr., ran for [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") as the candidate of the Conservative Party. Running only on the Conservative Party line and the Independent Alliance Party line, Buckley defeated Democratic Congressman [Richard Ottinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Ottinger "Richard Ottinger") and unelected incumbent Republican U.S. Senator [Charles Goodell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Goodell "Charles Goodell"), receiving 39% of the vote.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-6) Buckley served one term in the Senate.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-7) According to the _New York Post_, "Buckley's victory cemented, for a time, an electoral coalition of urban, ethnic Democrats with rural and suburban Republicans—all disgusted with excessive taxation, runaway government spending and the decline of traditional values."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto2-5) In [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_election_in_New_York,_1976 "United States Senate election in New York, 1976"), Buckley ran for reelection to the U.S. Senate as the candidate of the Republican and Conservative parties, losing to Democrat [Daniel Patrick Moynihan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Patrick_Moynihan "Daniel Patrick Moynihan").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-8)

In 1978, registered Conservative [William Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Carney_(politician) "William Carney (politician)"), a member of the [Suffolk County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suffolk_County,_New_York "Suffolk County, New York") legislature, was elected to the [United States House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") in [New York's 1st congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York's_1st_congressional_district "New York's 1st congressional district"), a long-time Democratic stronghold on [Long Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island "Long Island"), after winning the Republican primary and running on both party lines.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-9) He eventually served four terms before retiring.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-10)

### 1980s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1980s")]

In 1980, the Conservative Party endorsed [Al D'Amato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_D'Amato "Al D'Amato") in a [U.S. Senate race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_election_in_New_York,_1980 "United States Senate election in New York, 1980") in which he successfully challenged incumbent Sen. [Jacob Javits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Javits "Jacob Javits") in a Republican primary.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-11) D'Amato then narrowly prevailed in the general election over Democrat [Elizabeth Holtzman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Holtzman "Elizabeth Holtzman"); the 275,100 votes D'Amato received on the Conservative line exceeded his slim margin of victory.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-13)

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/William_Carney.png/250px-William_Carney.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_Carney.png)

[William Carney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Carney_(politician) "William Carney (politician)") represented [New York's 1st congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York's_1st_congressional_district "New York's 1st congressional district") as a member of the Conservative Party from 1979 to 1985.

In the [1982 gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_New_York_gubernatorial_election "1982 New York gubernatorial election"), the party nominated Republican [Lewis Lehrman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Lehrman "Lewis Lehrman"),[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-14) who was narrowly defeated by Democrat [Mario Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cuomo "Mario Cuomo").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-15) In the [1986 gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_New_York_gubernatorial_election "1986 New York gubernatorial election"), the party nominated Republican [Andrew P. O'Rourke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_P._O'Rourke "Andrew P. O'Rourke"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-16) who was defeated by Cuomo in a landslide.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-17)

### 1990s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1990s")]

[Herbert London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_London "Herbert London") was the Conservative Party's nominee for Governor of New York in [1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_New_York_gubernatorial_election "1990 New York gubernatorial election"); that year, the party broke from the Republican Party, declining to cross-endorse Republican nominee [Pierre Rinfret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Rinfret "Pierre Rinfret").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-:0-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-19) Conservatives leaders cited Rinfret's support for abortion, his perceived lack of seriousness about his candidacy, and his potential difficulties in attacking incumbent Democratic Governor Mario Cuomo on fiscal policies as reasons for their decision to support London instead.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-:0-18) London ran a strong campaign statewide and finished one percentage point behind Rinfret, while Democratic Governor [Mario Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cuomo "Mario Cuomo") easily won re-election.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-20)

The party declined to endorse Republican [Rudy Giuliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani") for Mayor of New York City in his successful [1993](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_New_York_City_mayoral_election "1993 New York City mayoral election") and [1997](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_New_York_City_mayoral_election "1997 New York City mayoral election") campaigns. In each of those elections, Giuliani accepted the endorsement of the Liberal Party. The Conservative Party endorsed George Marlin for Mayor in 1993 and left its line blank in the 1997 New York City mayoral race.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto-2)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-22)

The party endorsed Republican George Pataki in his successful 1994 campaign to unseat incumbent Democratic Gov. [Mario Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Cuomo "Mario Cuomo"). In that race, Pataki "drew more than 300,000 votes on the Conservative line, double his slender winning margin over Mr. Cuomo."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto-2)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-23)

### 2000s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2000s")]

The party ran its own candidates for Mayor of New York City in the [2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_New_York_City_mayoral_election "2001 New York City mayoral election"),[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-24)[2005](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_New_York_City_mayoral_election "2005 New York City mayoral election"),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-25) and [2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_New_York_City_mayoral_election "2009 New York City mayoral election"),[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-26) declining to support successful Republican candidate [Michael Bloomberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bloomberg "Michael Bloomberg").

[John Spencer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Spencer_(mayor) "John Spencer (mayor)"), a former mayor of [Yonkers, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yonkers,_New_York "Yonkers, New York"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-27) was nominated for U.S. Senate by the Republican and Conservative Parties in the [2006 Senate election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate_election_in_New_York,_2006 "United States Senate election in New York, 2006") against [Hillary Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hillary_Clinton "Hillary Clinton"). Spencer was defeated by Clinton.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-28)

In the 2006 race for governor, Conservative Party Chairman Michael Long endorsed [John Faso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Faso "John Faso"), the former Assembly Minority Leader and Republican [State Comptroller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_State_Comptroller "New York State Comptroller") nominee in 2002.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-29) Faso won the nomination at the Republican convention, defeating former Massachusetts Gov. [Bill Weld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Weld "William Weld"), 61–39%.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-30) Following the convention, Weld withdrew from the race as senior party officials (including state Republican chairman [Stephen Minarik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Minarik "Stephen Minarik"), who endorsed Weld) urged party unity.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-31) In the general election, Faso was the nominee of both the Republican and Conservative parties,[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-32) but was defeated by [Eliot Spitzer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Spitzer "Eliot Spitzer").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-33)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/New_York%27s_23rd_congressional_district_special_election%2C_2009_results_by_county.svg/330px-New_York%27s_23rd_congressional_district_special_election%2C_2009_results_by_county.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_York's_23rd_congressional_district_special_election,_2009_results_by_county.svg)

2009 special election results, New York's 23rd congressional district

The Conservative Party nominated Republican candidates [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") and [Sarah Palin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Palin "Sarah Palin") for president and vice president in the [2008 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election "2008 United States presidential election"), which was won by Democrat [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") and [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-34)

The Conservative Party nominated [Doug Hoffman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doug_Hoffman "Doug Hoffman") for the [2009 special election in New York's 23rd congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_New_York's_23rd_congressional_district_special_election "2009 New York's 23rd congressional district special election"), an election won by the Democratic nominee, [Bill Owens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Owens_(New_York_politician) "Bill Owens (New York politician)").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-35) The Conservative Party chose Hoffman, a fiscal and social conservative, in reaction to the Republican Party's nomination of pro-choice, pro-same-sex-marriage, pro-union Assemblymember [Dede Scozzafava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dede_Scozzafava "Dede Scozzafava"), who Chairman Mike Long declared to be a "nice lady who is too liberal."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-36) On October 31, 2009, Scozzafava suspended her campaign,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-37) leading prominent Republicans such as national chairman [Michael Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Steele "Michael Steele") to endorse Hoffman.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-38) On Election Day, Owens prevailed over Hoffman by a margin of 48.3% to 46%.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-39) The 2009 special election received significant national attention, and was alternately described as "a referendum on President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama")" and "a fight over the [identity of the Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Factions_in_the_Republican_Party_(United_States) "Factions in the Republican Party (United States)")."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-wsyr1-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-nytimes110409-41) According to one commentator, "tea party conservatives see the GOP loss as a victory for conservativism over mere political party loyalty. They're describing the defeat as a warning shot fired in defense of principle."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-42) In addition, elected officials and observers opined that the congressional race affected the New York State Senate's December 2, 2009 vote against same-sex marriage legislation.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-44)

### 2010s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2010s")]

Party Chairman Michael Long endorsed [Rick Lazio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Lazio "Rick Lazio") for the [2010 New York gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_New_York_gubernatorial_election "2010 New York gubernatorial election") and directed his allies to do the same. However, several county chairmen instead coalesced behind vice chairman [Ralph Lorigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Lorigo?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ralph Lorigo (page does not exist)").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-45) Lazio defeated Lorigo in the primary election by a roughly 60–40% margin, but was defeated by [Carl Paladino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Paladino "Carl Paladino") in the Republican primary.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-46) Lazio dropped out of the race on September 27, requiring a vacancy committee to convene and select a replacement for him on the Conservative line.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-47) Long eventually endorsed Paladino and the vacancy committee followed, placing Paladino on the Conservative Party line. Paladino lost the general election,[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-48) but drew 232,264 votes on the Conservative Party line,[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-49) which allowed the party to overtake the [Independence Party of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Party_of_New_York "Independence Party of New York") and retake Row C (the third place ballot position in New York elections) for the first time since the 1998 elections.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-50) The party has held Row C ever since.

Prior to the passage of [same-sex marriage legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_Equality_Act_(New_York) "Marriage Equality Act (New York)") in 2011, Long stated that the party would not endorse any candidate who supported same-sex marriage.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-ny-52) Four Republican state senators—Sens. [James Alesi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Alesi "James Alesi"), [Mark Grisanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Grisanti "Mark Grisanti"), [Roy McDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_McDonald_(politician) "Roy McDonald (politician)"), and [Stephen Saland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Saland "Stephen Saland")—voted in favor of same-sex marriage. Alesi did not seek re-election in 2012,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-53) while Grisanti, McDonald, and Saland faced challengers in 2012 who received the Conservative Party's endorsement. Grisanti was re-elected to the State Senate,[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-54) while McDonald was defeated in a Republican primary[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto3-55) and Saland was defeated in a general election in which a Conservative Party-endorsed challenger acted as a spoiler.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto4-56)

State Senator [Mark Grisanti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Grisanti "Mark Grisanti"), the last remaining Republican state senator to have voted for the Marriage Equality Act, was again denied Conservative Party endorsement in 2014; the party instead endorsed [dummy candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_candidate "Dummy candidate") Timothy Gallagher in State Senate District 60. Grisanti lost the Republican primary, but remained in the general election on the [Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independence_Party_of_New_York "Independence Party of New York") line. In the general election, Gallagher—despite not campaigning at all—won 8 percent of the vote; the vote split between Gallagher, Grisanti, and Republican candidate Kevin Stocker allowed Democrat [Marc Panepinto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc_Panepinto "Marc Panepinto") to win the election with only 34 percent of the vote.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-58)

The Party endorsed [Rob Astorino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Astorino "Rob Astorino") very early in the [2014 gubernatorial election process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_York_gubernatorial_election "2014 New York gubernatorial election").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-freddicker21014-59) In the election for New York State Comptroller, the party threatened to nominate its own candidate if the Republicans could not find a candidate from their party to run on the line;[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-60) the GOP eventually nominated [Onondaga County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onondaga_County,_New_York "Onondaga County, New York") Comptroller Rob Antonacci.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-61)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/61/Donald_J._Trump_at_Marriott_Marquis_NYC_September_7th_2016_15.jpg/250px-Donald_J._Trump_at_Marriott_Marquis_NYC_September_7th_2016_15.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Donald_J._Trump_at_Marriott_Marquis_NYC_September_7th_2016_15.jpg)

Then Presidential Candidate [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") accepting the Conservative nomination at the [New York Marriott Marquis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Marriott_Marquis "New York Marriott Marquis") on September 7, 2016

In 2016, the Conservative Party nominated eventual winner [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") for President of the United States[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-62) under a New York election law that allows multiple parties to nominate the same ticket.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-63)

[![Image 14](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/42/Mike_Long%2C_Jim_McLaughlin_and_Graham_Shafer_%281618980902%29_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mike_Long,_Jim_McLaughlin_and_Graham_Shafer_(1618980902)_(cropped).jpg)

[Michael Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_R._Long "Michael R. Long") served as the chairman of the party for over 30 years, from 1988 to 2019.

On April 13, 2018, the Conservative Party executive committee selected [Marcus Molinaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Molinaro "Marcus Molinaro") as its candidate in the [2018 gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_New_York_gubernatorial_election "2018 New York gubernatorial election") in what Long termed a "not very easy" decision; the party chose Molinaro over Deputy State Senate Majority Leader [John A. DeFrancisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._DeFrancisco "John A. DeFrancisco") and openly refused to consider [Erie County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erie_County,_New_York "Erie County, New York") Executive [Joel Giambra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joel_Giambra "Joel Giambra").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-64)

The Conservative Party of [Cattaraugus County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattaraugus_County,_New_York "Cattaraugus County, New York") is alleged to have been the target of a [hostile takeover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_raiding "Party raiding") by members of the Republican Party, after 37 former Republicans abruptly changed party registration in October 2017. County party chairman Leonard Ciros alleged that the Republican Party violated state party loyalty laws and the federal [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racketeer_Influenced_and_Corrupt_Organizations_Act "Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-65)

As of 2018, the Party holds "Row C" on New York ballots—the third-place ballot position, directly below the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") and [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") parties—because it received the third-highest number of votes of any political party in the 2010,[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-66) 2014,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-67) and 2018[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-68) gubernatorial elections.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-69)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-71)

Long announced his retirement from the chairmanship of the Conservative Party on January 28, 2019 after having served in that role for 30 years.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-72) In February 2019, he was elected Chairman Emeritus of the Party.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-73) On February 23, 2019, the Party named Gerard Kassar of Brooklyn as its new chairman.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-74)

### 2020s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2020s")]

In 2020, the Conservative Party nominated incumbent Republican President Donald Trump for re-election to the presidency.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-75) Trump was defeated by Democrat [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-76) In 2021, the Conservative Party successfully teamed up with the Republican Party to raise opposition among the state's voters and defeat three ballot initiatives proposed by Democrats.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-77)

During the [2022 New York gubernatorial election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_New_York_gubernatorial_election "2022 New York gubernatorial election") the party endorsed Republican [Lee Zeldin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Zeldin "Lee Zeldin") who had the best showing as a Republican for governor since 1970 earning 2,762,581 votes and losing to incumbent [Kathy Hochul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kathy_Hochul "Kathy Hochul") by just 6.39% of the vote.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-78)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-79)

On August 17, 2024, the Conservative Party nominated Donald Trump for President of the United States during the [2024 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-80)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-81)

The party ran its own candidates for Mayor of New York City in [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_New_York_City_mayoral_election "2021 New York City mayoral election") and [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_York_City_mayoral_election "2025 New York City mayoral election"). In 2024, Gonzalo Duran, Vice Chairman of the [Bronx Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronx_Conservative_Party?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bronx Conservative Party (page does not exist)"), petitioned for the mayoral candidacy but was not selected. He subsequently pivoted to run for Public Advocate of New York City, becoming the first Conservative candidate in over three election cycles to receive a cross-party endorsement in a citywide race.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-84)

## Strategy and reputation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Strategy and reputation")]

In 2012, _The New York Times_ stated that the Conservative Party had "a successful electoral record in a decidedly blue state in which the Conservatives have elbowed the Republican Party to the right".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto1-4) Also in 2012, the _New York Post_ asserted that the Party had "helped the GOP maintain its majority in the state Senate, even as New York has turned an ever-deeper blue over the last half century" and added that it had "forced the state Republican Party to (sometimes) remember what it stood for—by threatening its power".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto2-5)

Rather than nominating its own candidates, the Conservative Party usually endorses the same candidates as the Republican Party and campaigns against the Democratic candidates. However, the party has withheld support from Republican candidates if it deems them too liberal. For example, the Conservative Party withheld its support from Republican [Rudy Giuliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani")'s [fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fusion "Electoral fusion") campaigns with endorsement from the Liberal Party for New York City mayor in 1989, 1993[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-85) and 1997.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-86) In the [2004 U.S. Senate election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_Senate_election_in_New_York "2004 United States Senate election in New York"), the Conservative Party endorsed [Marilyn O'Grady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marilyn_O'Grady "Marilyn O'Grady") to oppose Republican candidate [Howard Mills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Mills "Howard Mills") and incumbent [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") Senator [Charles Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Schumer "Charles Schumer"). Also in 2004, the Party's decision to endorse Tom Dadey rather than incumbent Republican State Senator [Nancy Larraine Hoffmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Larraine_Hoffmann "Nancy Larraine Hoffmann") in State Senate District 49 helped bring about the victory of Democrat [David Valesky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Valesky "David Valesky") in that race. After losing to Hoffmann in the Republican primary, Dadey—with the support of the Conservative Party and the Independence Party—remained in the race; Hoffmann lost the general election by 742 votes.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-89)

Following the passage of [same-sex marriage legislation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_Equality_Act_(New_York) "Marriage Equality Act (New York)") in 2011, the Conservative Party stated that it would withdraw support for any candidate who had voted for the bill;[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-NYT07022011-90)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-ny-52) two Republican senators who voted for same-sex marriage—[Roy McDonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_J._McDonald "Roy J. McDonald") and [Stephen Saland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Saland "Stephen Saland")—lost their seats in 2012.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto3-55)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-auto4-56)

The party has also endorsed Democratic candidates, including controversial former [Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York")[mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_mayors_of_Buffalo,_New_York "List of mayors of Buffalo, New York") and presidential candidate [Jimmy Griffin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_D._Griffin "James D. Griffin"), who was initially elected mayor solely on the Conservative ticket but had Republican support as well for his subsequent campaigns. It also cross-endorsed such Democrats as Asms. [Michael Cusick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Cusick "Michael Cusick"),[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_of_New_York_State#cite_note-91)[Michael P.
